title: Genesis 29. The Cup of Labor.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 29. The Cup of Labor.
Then Jacob went on his journey and came to the land of the people of the east.
The man who left Beersheba with nothing arrives.
No servant.
No camels.
No gold.
No gifts.
The man who sent his servant with ten camels and jewelry of silver and gold to find Rebekah now walks into the same land on foot,
carrying nothing but the dream.
Abraham's servant arrived at the well with wealth.
Jacob arrives at the well with a stone pillow and a vow that starts with if.
He looked, and saw a well in the field.
Three flocks of sheep lying there by it.
The stone on the well's mouth was large.
The shepherds waited,
all the flocks had to be gathered before anyone could roll the stone.
Then they would water the sheep and put the stone back.
A well.
The same meeting place.
The well where Rebekah drew water for ten camels.
The well where Abraham's servant prayed.
The well at Beersheba where Isaac's men found water.
The well in the wilderness where Hagar was found.
The Cup is always near water.
While he was yet speaking with the shepherds,
Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was keeping them.
The same moment as chapter twenty-four.
The servant was praying.
Rebekah appeared.
Jacob is speaking.
Rachel appears.
The prayer is answered before it is spoken.
The woman is there before the man asks.
The Cup is already at the well.
When Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother,
and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother,
Jacob went near and rolled the stone from the well's mouth,
and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother.
He rolled the stone.
Alone.
The shepherds said it took all the flocks gathered to roll it.
Jacob rolls it by himself.
The same strength that seized a heel now opens a well.
The same hands that held goatskin now hold stone.
The man who took by deception now gives by labor.
He waters sheep that are not his,
for a woman he has just seen,
in a land where he owns nothing.
Jacob kissed Rachel and lifted up his voice and wept.
The man who calculated risk before deceiving his father now weeps without calculation.
The man who set conditions on God,
if You will be with me, now weeps because he has arrived.
He told Rachel who he was.
Rebekah's son.
Her cousin's son.
The family connection that Abraham's servant traveled to find,
Jacob stumbles into by the providence of a well and a shepherdess.
She ran and told her father.
Laban heard the news of Jacob, his sister's son,
and ran to meet him,
and embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house.
Jacob told Laban all these things.
Laban said: Surely you are my bone and my flesh.
Jacob stayed with him a month.
Then Laban said: Because you are my relative,
should you therefore serve me for nothing?
Tell me, what shall your wages be?
Laban has two daughters.
The name of the older was Leah,
and the name of the younger was Rachel.
Leah's eyes were weak.
Rachel was beautiful in form and attractive.
Jacob loved Rachel.
He said: I will serve you seven years for Rachel,
your younger daughter.
Seven years.
The man who took a birthright in a moment of hunger now offers seven years of labor for a woman.
The grabber becomes the server.
The one who stole now works.
The Cup that was taken by deception is now sought by sweat.
The man who would not wait for God to fulfill the oracle now waits seven years for a wife.
Something has changed.
Not completely, not cleanly.
But the man who said if is now saying I will serve.
Laban said:
It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to another man.
Stay with me.
Jacob served seven years for Rachel.
They seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.
A few days.
The man who could not wait for stew now waits seven years and calls them short.
The same Jacob who grabbed a heel, grabbed a birthright,
grabbed a blessing, waits.
Love does what fear and ambition could not.
It makes the grabber patient.
The Cup that was seized is now pursued through labor,
and the labor is light because of love.
Jacob said to Laban: Give me my wife,
for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her.
Laban gathered all the men of the place and made a feast.
In the evening,
he took Leah his daughter and brought her to Jacob.
Jacob went in to her.
Laban gave Zilpah his servant to his daughter Leah as a servant.
In the morning, behold, it was Leah.
The deceiver is deceived.
The man who dressed in his brother's clothing and brought his father a meal he did not hunt is now given a wife he did not choose.
The man who exploited darkness, coming to his blind father at night,
is now exploited by darkness.
The wedding feast was real.
The celebration was real.
The night was real.
But the woman in the dark was not the woman he loved.
What you do follows you.
The pattern comes back.
Jacob put goatskins on his arms to fool his blind father.
Laban puts a veil on Leah to fool a seeing man in the dark.
Jacob said I am Esau.
Laban says: Here is Rachel.
The same lie.
The same darkness.
The same substitution of the older for the younger.
He said to Laban: What is this you have done to me?
Did I not serve with you for Rachel?
Why then have you deceived me?
The word, deceived, is the same root as Jacob's name.
to deceive, to mislead.
The deceiver names the deception.
The man whose name means heel-catcher is caught by the heel.
The pattern he set in motion, the older serving the younger,
the younger taking the older's place, is turned back on him.
He took Esau's place.
Now Leah has taken Rachel's place.
Laban said: It is not done so in our place,
to give the younger before the firstborn.
The exact words.
The younger before the firstborn.
The exact thing Jacob did to Esau,
taking the younger's blessing before the firstborn's,
is now named by Laban as the reason for the deception.
The uncle who never met Jacob until this month knows the customs.
And the custom, the older before the younger,
is the one Jacob violated.
Laban does not know about Esau.
But the pattern knows.
The Cup that was stolen returns as a Cup that is withheld.
The vessel that deceived is now deceived by the same mechanism.
Laban said: Fulfill the week of this one,
and we will give you the other also,
for the service which you will serve with me for seven more years.
Jacob did so.
He fulfilled her week.
Laban gave him Rachel his daughter as wife.
Laban gave Bilhah his servant to his daughter Rachel as a servant.
He went in also to Rachel,
and he loved Rachel more than Leah,
and served with him seven more years.
Fourteen years.
Seven for Leah, whom he did not love.
Seven for Rachel, whom he did.
The man who grabbed a birthright in one afternoon now works fourteen years for two wives.
The grabber has become the laborer.
The Cup of labor is the Cup that fills through serving,
not through taking.
The man who could not wait for God now waits longer than he ever imagined.
The Lord saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb.
But Rachel was barren.
The same pattern.
Sarah barren while Hagar bore.
Rebekah barren for twenty years.
Now Rachel barren while Leah bears.
The Cup that was always held by a barren woman now rests in a tent where the unloved wife is fertile,
and the loved wife is not.
The God who opened wombs in Gerar and answered Isaac's prayer now opens the womb of the woman Jacob did not want.
Leah conceived and bore a son.
She named him Reuben, for she said:
Because the Lord has looked at my affliction.
For now my husband will love me.
Reuben, See, a son.
Or: the Lord has seen.
The first son of Jacob is named by a mother who is watching to see if her husband notices.
The Cup of promise, offspring like dust,
begins with a woman naming her son as a prayer for love.
Not for the covenant.
Not for the promise.
For love.
The unloved wife wants to be seen.
She conceived again and bore a son.
She said: Because the Lord has heard that I am hated,
He has given me this one also.
She named him Simeon.
Simeon, Hearing.
The Lord has heard.
The second son is named for the God who listens.
The same verb used when God heard Ishmael's voice in the wilderness.
The God who hears is now hearing the voice of a woman who is hated in her own household.
She conceived again and bore a son.
She said: Now this time my husband will be joined to me,
because I have borne him three sons.
Therefore his name was called Levi.
Levi, Joined.
Attached.
The third son is named for the bond Leah wants and does not have.
Three sons.
Three prayers.
Each name is a cry: see me, hear me, join me.
The Cup of promise is producing sons,
but the vessel naming them is naming them for what she does not have.
She conceived again and bore a son.
She said: This time I will praise the Lord.
Therefore she named him Judah.
Then she stopped bearing.
Judah, Praise.
The fourth son.
The name changes.
Reuben was see me.
Simeon was hear me.
Levi was join me.
Judah is not a request.
It is a response.
The woman who asked for her husband's love three times and did not receive it stops asking.
She turns from Jacob to God.
Not because she is loved.
Because she has decided to praise.
And Judah is the line.
The Cup of the covenant,
the promise that all nations will be blessed through Abraham's offspring,
will not pass through Rachel's son.
It will pass through Leah's.
Through the woman no one chose.
Through the wife who was given in the dark.
Through the mother who named her son not for what she wanted but for what she would give.
The cup of labor produces a son named praise,
from the woman no one loved.
The Cup holds.
The vessel is learning, slowly, painfully,
through labor and deception and tears and the unloved wife's prayers.
The man who stole is now the man who serves.
The deceiver is now the deceived.
The grabber is now the worker.
The conditional if of Bethel is being tested by fourteen years of labor for a woman he loves and a woman he does not.
And through it all, through the dark, through the substitution,
through the barrenness and the fertility, the Cup produces.
Not where the vessel expected.
But where God opened.
